Subject: Re: Production errors + latency spike (CedarBank) — post-incident summary and recommendations

Hi all — wrapping up with a concise post-incident note and a recommended playbook to prevent recurrence. Summary of findings: 

- Root cause: transient headroom exhaustion in CedarBank’s reserved capacity pool triggered by an atypical burst of long-sequence requests from two internal CedarBank services. One dedicated host experienced heavy KV cache churn (evictions + rehydration) which amplified tail latencies and led to request queueing across the pool.
- Impact: elevated 5xx (mostly timeout) rate for ~45 minutes; p95 latency increased to ~1.2s at peak; CedarBank saw request throttling and degraded throughput for production routes.

Immediate mitigations performed during incident:
- Enabled automatic fallback to burst pool for the impacted tenant (reduced client-visible latency within ~2 minutes).
- Brought an extra dedicated worker online (recovered capacity in ~6 minutes).
- Temporarily relaxed concurrency caps to reduce queueing while headroom was restored.

Recommendations (short-term + medium-term):
1) Short-term: Enable automatic fallback-to-burst for CedarBank during peak windows (controlled rollout) and pre-warm an extra reserved worker when a sudden headroom spike is detected.
2) Medium-term: Implement per-route KV cache isolation to prevent single-route cache churn from affecting entire reserved pools.
3) Runbook changes: add an explicit step to check for long-sequence / high-kv eviction patterns in the first 5 minutes of any headroom alert.
4) Business ops: propose a one-week trial of automatic fallback with an SLA credit waiver option if CedarBank prefers manual control.

I’ll circulate a short action tracker with owners and ETA for each recommendation. Priya — happy to present this to CedarBank’s execs if you want a technical deep-dive.

Karthik Iyer
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
